dek: A small trial of adults under 45 tested an intensive diet and exercise program. Here is what it found, and what it does not prove.

slides.label: Why it matters
slides.text: About *38 million Americans* have type 2 diabetes, and more *younger adults* are being diagnosed every year.

slides.label: The study
slides.text: The *RESET for Remission* trial followed *96 adults ages 18 to 45*, diagnosed within the past six years.

slides.label: The program
slides.text: A *medically supervised* low-calorie diet plus supervised workouts that combined *cardio and strength training*.

slides.label: The result
slides.text: *54%* reached remission after six months, versus *4%* with usual care. Grip strength rose about *8%*.

slides.label: The limits
slides.text: Small, short and intensive, with medical teams watching closely. *Six months of remission is not a cure.*

slides.label: The Den's take
slides.text: Not a crash diet. The takeaway anyone can use: *strength training* helps muscles pull sugar from the blood. *Ask your doctor.*

yt_title: Can Diet and Exercise Reverse Type 2 Diabetes? New Study
caption_instagram:
Type 2 diabetes remission study: 54% of younger adults in an intensive diet and exercise program reached remission in six months, versus 4% with usual care. 💪

The RESET for Remission trial followed 96 adults ages 18 to 45 who were diagnosed within the past six years. The program combined a medically supervised low-calorie diet with supervised cardio and strength training, and participants kept their muscle while losing fat.

The limits matter: it was small, short and intensive, and six months of remission is not a cure.

The takeaway anyone can use: strength training helps your muscles pull sugar out of your blood. Bring this study to your doctor.

caption_facebook:
A new study in The Lancet Regional Health, Americas, tested whether intensive diet and exercise could put early type 2 diabetes into remission. In the RESET for Remission trial, 96 adults ages 18 to 45 with recent diagnoses were split into an intensive program or usual care.

After six months, 54% of the program group reached remission, compared with 4% of the usual-care group. The program was medically supervised and included strength training, which helped participants keep muscle while losing fat.

The researchers note real limits: a small group, six months of follow-up and a demanding program. If you live with type 2 diabetes, bring it to your doctor. This is general information, not medical advice.
caption_linkedin:
A new trial puts a number on what lifestyle change can do for early type 2 diabetes. In the RESET for Remission study, 54% of adults under 45 in an intensive, medically supervised diet and exercise program reached remission after six months, versus 4% with usual care.

Two details stand out for employers and health leaders: participants were younger adults, a group being diagnosed at rising rates, and strength training helped them keep muscle while losing fat. The program was also intensive and supported by full medical teams, which is the hard part to scale.
